nodes.text: We say that “voltage drops” across a resistor.
The current is the same at A and B!
The current is lower through this whole circuit due to the resistor.

nodes.detailed_figure_description: A closed-loop circuit is drawn as a traffic-jam analogy. Small rectangular vehicles or particles marked “e⁻” crowd around the loop. A zigzag resistor labeled R is at the top, and a battery labeled V is at the bottom, with a plus sign on the left terminal and a minus sign on the right terminal.
nodes.figure_alternative: Circuit diagram using crowded e⁻ symbols as a traffic-jam model, with resistor R and voltage source V.

nodes.text: A flashlight bulb draws 300mA from its 1.5 V battery. What’s the resistance of the bulb? If the battery degrades and only produces 1.2 V how would the current change?

nodes.figure_alternative: Hand-drawn flashlight with a glowing bulb.

nodes.spoken_math_alternative: I equals V divided by R, so R equals V divided by I, which equals 1.5 volts divided by 0.30 amperes, or 5.0 ohms.
For V changing to 1.2 volts, I equals 1.2 volts divided by 5.0 ohms, which equals 0.24 amperes, or 240 milliamperes.
